html:
Subak is the system by which Balinese farmers share water among their terraced rice fields. Each subak is an association of farmers who draw water from one source; they meet at water temples to decide when to plant and how to divide the flow. Inscriptions from the late 800s already mention irrigated rice fields on Bali.

Water runs from crater lakes and rivers through tunnels and canals down the slopes. Temples at every level, from the great lake temples to small field shrines, set the calendar. The system expresses Tri Hita Karana, the Balinese idea of harmony among people, gods and nature.

The anthropologist J. Stephen Lansing showed that the temple schedules do practical work: by having neighbouring subaks plant at the same time, they leave fields fallow together and starve pests. When the Green Revolution of the 1970s told farmers to plant as often as possible, pest outbreaks followed, and the old schedules were partly restored. UNESCO listed the subak landscape as World Heritage in 2012.
